claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential can be trained on strategically sampled ab initio data for both solid and liquid multicomponent alloys.
Such a potential can substantially reduce the cost of computing solid and liquid free energies and fusion properties relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The proposed workflow can retain near-ab-initio fidelity for fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The training configurations should span room temperature through temperatures above melting and cover both crystalline and liquid regimes.
The training data must consistently represent electronic contributions and anharmonic vibrations to preserve high-temperature thermodynamic relevance.
The machine-learning potential must achieve near-ab-initio force accuracy in both solid and liquid structures.
Accurate forces across the melting transition enable evaluation of solid and liquid free energies.
Reproducing ab initio energies and forces allows classical or accelerated simulations to converge free-energy calculations at a fraction of the cost of ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD.
The machine-learning potential can include corrections for electron–vibration coupling.
The machine-learning potential can retain anharmonic contributions sufficiently to reproduce temperature-dependent thermodynamic properties.
The workflow should reduce computational cost by at least one order of magnitude.
The workflow may provide an approximately 100-fold cost reduction.
Solid–liquid free-energy differences, fusion enthalpies, and transition temperatures should remain within approximately 5–10% of ab initio results.
The method is applicable to alloys containing up to five or six components.
The proposed temperature domain extends from ambient conditions to the alloy liquidus region.
Insufficient sampling of the liquid or near-melting phase space can produce larger prediction errors.
Inadequate treatment of electron–vibration coupling can produce larger errors in predicted high-temperature properties.
A discrepancy greater than 10% in fusion enthalpy or solid–liquid free-energy difference, or failure to reproduce melting temperature within 5–10%, would falsify the hypothesis.
